As a kid, I dreamed of becoming an astronaut, but instead I decided to try Counter-Strike 2… and I still went to space – just because of the Desert Eagle’s recoil.    CS2 made me realize my reactions are slower than my grandma’s internet connection when she’s watching YouTube on mobile data. I join a match hoping to get at least one kill, but I end up with 0/17 and the MVP award for “most beautiful fall after a headshot.”    The graphics are amazing – you can see every detail, even your tears hitting the keyboard after someone with the nickname “xXx\_P3pSiM4n\_xXx” stabs you in the back. The new Source 2 engine is so realistic that when I throw a flashbang, I get blinded in real life… and my upstairs neighbor is now asking why I’m screaming “BLIND!!!” in the middle of the night.    The gun mechanics are unique – mine always shoots sideways, while my opponent’s gun has a built-in GPS that guides every bullet straight into my forehead. The smoke is “dynamic,” which means I can’t see anything… except for the enemy, who can apparently see perfectly through it because he’s graduated from Hogwarts and mastered the spell “Wallhackus Maximus.”    CS2 has taught me some valuable life lessons:    * Never run with a knife… unless you want to die faster.  * Never trust a “teammate” who says “EZ WIN” at the start of the round.  * And most importantly: life is short, but the defuse-without-a-kit animation is eternal.    I love this game because every match is different – sometimes I die in 3 seconds, sometimes in 5. Sometimes we win, but that happens so rarely it feels like spotting a unicorn.    I recommend CS2 to anyone who wants to test their patience, nervous system, and how hard they can slam a desk before it breaks.

CS2 Review – Great Game, But the Cheaters & Trust Factor Suck  CS2 is honestly a blast to play. The gunplay feels super clean, movement is smooth, and the mechanics are the best in pvp shooter games. new subtick system is meh and 64 tick would be better with shots registering however it works decent enough so cant complain much . obviously graphics revamp being good  Gameplay-wise, it’s top-tier. Whether you’re clutching a 1v4 or lining up perfect utility, the game really rewards skill and timing. It feels good to play — when it works properly.  But here’s the catch: cheaters are everywhere, and it kills the experience fast. Even in Prime, you'll still run into spinbots, wallers, or people that just feel off. VAC Live doesn’t seem to be catching much in real-time, and it’s honestly frustrating when you’re trying to play legit.  And then there's the Trust Factor system, which seems completely messed up. If you’re on a newer account or haven’t dumped thousands of hours into Steam, good luck. You'll get thrown into lobbies with blatant cheaters or super toxic teammates while older accounts with shady pasts get better games. It feels super biased and makes playing on a fresh or clean account feel like a punishment.  Overall, CS2 is a great game at its core, but the matchmaking experience needs serious fixing. If Valve ever sorts out the cheaters and reworks Trust Factor to be fairer, this game would be unstoppable.  8/10 – Amazing gameplay, but ruined too often by cheaters and bad matchmaking.

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike and staying up until 3AM trying to clutch one more round. For over two decades, this franchise has been a constant in my life — a place of competition, camaraderie, heartbreak, and triumph. So when CS2 was announced, I felt a rush of excitement mixed with fear. Could it possibly live up to the legacy?  It didn’t just live up. It evolved.  The moment I loaded into the new engine, I felt it. The crispness of the movement, the responsive gunplay, the lighting that makes every map feel alive — it’s all there. But more importantly, the soul of Counter-Strike is intact. The tension, the strategy, the adrenaline rush of a 1v3 clutch — CS2 delivers all of it, but with a polish that finally reflects the greatness the series has always deserved.  What moved me the most, though, was how familiar it still felt. Stepping onto Dust II again felt like walking into a childhood home that had been beautifully renovated. The layout is the same, the memories echo in the corners, but everything looks and feels better. Sharper. More alive.  There are still things to be improved — bugs, matchmaking quirks, balance issues — but those are scars that any living game wears with time. What matters is the foundation is rock solid. CS2 isn’t a reboot. It’s a love letter. To the veterans who remember 1.6. To the Global Elite grinders. To the first-time players discovering the thrill of their first ace.  To me, Counter-Strike 2 is a reminder of why I fell in love with gaming in the first place.  Thank you, Valve. This one means something.  I have quitted this game but thank you  Valve for everything

This game saved my life.  I am 30.  My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.  When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.  After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.  Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I've been a long-time Counter-Strike player and was genuinely disappointed with how CS2 replaced CS:GO. While I appreciate the addition of dynamic smokes, most of the gameplay changes have negatively impacted the experience for me.    Performance has noticeably declined — where I used to get 400+ FPS on certain maps in CS:GO, I now struggle to get stable frames in CS2. Hit registration feels inconsistent, movement is clunky, and the peeker's advantage is too strong, making it hard to hold angles reliably.    The removal of Overwatch and reliance on VAC Live has not helped with the cheating problem. There's a real need for a better anti-cheat system, as matches often feel compromised.    I'm also frustrated by the decision to remove CS:GO entirely, unlike how Source and 1.6 were kept separate in the past. Many of us would have preferred CS2 to be its own game instead of a forced upgrade.    The map rotation choices are also questionable. Personally, I loved Anubis and was disappointed to see it removed instead of a less popular map like Dust2.    Finally, I hope Valve starts putting more resources into improving core gameplay and listening to player feedback, rather than focusing so heavily on monetization through skins and cases.    I keep playing because I’ve invested so much time into this series, but I honestly don’t enjoy it like I used to. I miss CS:GO.

Counter-Strike 2 Review: Volumetric Smokes and the Need to Move On    Counter-Strike 2 is a slick, high-friction reinvention of a game that never really needed fixing. And yet, somehow, it works. Movement feels tight, gunplay is brutally efficient, and the new Source 2 engine adds a strange, almost hypnotic energy to the maps—like they’re alive, humming under your feet, quietly urging you to make a move to someplace a little more right for you.    That’s always been the spirit of CS: finding the right place, at the right time, with the right angle. A town, maybe. A town to keep you groovin’. One that rewards quick decisions, sharp reflexes, and a willingness to talk about it—over and over again. Mid push? Talk about it. Utility timing? Talk about it. Solo queueing? You're gonna talk about it all night in Discord.    And when the round begins, you don’t just run—you move on. There’s something rhythmic about it. You’ve got to move. You’ve got to move. The tempo in your head isn’t just adrenaline; it’s that quiet compulsion to rotate fast, to peak the corner just so, to listen for audio cues like you’re tuning a groove.    And whether you’re carrying bombsite A or just holding garage with a Nova and a dream, there's that persistent voice, subtle but steady: Won’t you take me there? Maybe not in words—but in vibe. You know it. You've felt it. A place where your shots land and your pings stabilize. A better ping. A better round. A better town. The right town.    The maps? Sharper, glossier. Mirage feels like it got a deep tissue massage. Dust2 still smells like home—burnt rubber, broken dreams, and flashbangs. Inferno? It’s a place with energy, with momentum. A place you want to stay in, but also... move through. Something about it just makes you want to keep grooving.    It’s not perfect. You’ll get tilted. You’ll get eco’d. You’ll get absolutely deleted by someone whose entire personality is bound to their butterfly knife skin. But you’ll load back in. Every time. Hoping—begging, really—that maybe this round, your team will finally take you there.    Somewhere new.  Somewhere smoother.  Somewhere funkier.    8.5/10  Valve didn’t just remaster CS—they whispered to the soul of every solo-queued player: Won’t you take me to a better game?  And then they did.  Welcome to CS2.

The July 29 CS2 update introduced more problems than improvements, and most of the changes feel rushed, untested, and disconnected from what players actually want.    Movement/Bhop is broken  Previously, you could jump from any surface by timing your second jump (bhop mechanic). Now, that second jump doesn't always register, even with perfect timing. It feels like there's artificial input delay or a cooldown on air movement. This ruins the flow and skill expression of movement. Bring back consistent bhop behavior — it was part of CS's identity.    Skin bugs (black textures and visual glitches)  Many skins — especially Field-Tested or Battle-Scarred — now appear covered in black patches or broken textures. It literally looks like someone pasted the wrong material onto the skin. This destroys the appeal of skins and affects items people paid real money for.    Weapon animations are buggy and overdone  AnimGraph2 is a cool idea, but it was poorly implemented. When inspecting the AK-47, the character's hand clips through the weapon. It looks broken. Animations feel overcomplicated and janky instead of smooth and satisfying.    The shooting mechanics were changed again — why?  CS2 shooting was already controversial, but people adjusted. Now it's changed again — the recoil timing feels different, bullets feel delayed, and spraying feels wrong. Why keep changing core shooting mechanics after players already adapted?    AK-47 draw sound is awful  The new draw sound for the AK-47 is flat-out unpleasant. It doesn’t sound powerful or clean — just off. This is a small thing, but sound in CS has always been critical, and this one feels like a downgrade.    Please stop reinventing core mechanics and visuals every patch. Fix what’s broken, but don’t constantly alter fundamentals that define Counter-Strike.

Why would a video game company who is known for their outstanding support for their legacy releases suddenly stop supporting their biggest multiplayer title and push out an unfinished game in it's place.  Why would a video game company who is known for their amazing attention to detail and features not include a number of features such as factions, clan tags, game modes, maps, and other details in their game? Even after 2 years from its launch not only have many of these features that were originally promised and assumed to remain not made their way into the game. But other features that weren't requested such as distracting animations, sub-tick, and MR12 have been added in instead along with a number of updates that continue to push this e-sports title out as a experimental test game rather than a functional multiplayer experience. Every new update breaks an old feature weather that be demos/replays, input delay, animation/sound queues, or sub tick affecting movement.   While Valve is no doubt under a lot of pressure to deliver a smooth experience for everyone who plays their game and has a bold reputation to uphold. It's very upsetting seeing them so unsure of what to do with the case of Counter Strike. With such a diverse and split community, every single change and update will have varying opinions regardless of what game it is. But despite Counter Strike's massive community, generally speaking most players are united with the thought that overall, Counter Strike 2 is an inferior game to it's predecessor. Dear Valve,    Thank you. Truly. It takes a special kind of genius to simultaneously create one of the most legendary FPS franchises of all time and manage to fumble it at nearly every opportunity.    You gave us Counter-Strike — a game built on precision, skill, and tension. Then you gave us Counter-Strike 2 — a game built on... shattered promises, tick-rate cope, and smoke grenades with more processing power than Half-Life: Alyx.    Let’s break it down:    Communication: Or more accurately, the complete lack of it. Other devs do roadmaps, dev blogs, Twitter updates. You? You drop a patch with one sentence and vanish like you're working from Black Mesa after a resonance cascade. Are the devs okay? Blink twice in morse code if you need help.    Anticheat: VAC is so ineffective it might as well stand for "Virtually Assuring Cheaters." Do you just throw darts at a wall to decide bans? Because right now, it feels like you’ve outsourced anticheat to a Magic 8-Ball.    Matchmaking: The Premier system is like a luxury car with no wheels. Nice dashboard, clean look — but where are we going? Smurfs, cheaters, one-sided matchmaking, no party restrictions… It's almost impressive how bad it feels. At least FACEIT still works (thanks, third-party devs for doing your job for you).    Pro Scene Support: Esports? You mean the thing you kind of support sometimes, unless it requires any structure, promotion, or actual effort? Meanwhile, Riot’s out here building entire leagues while you’re still deciding if you want to tweet about your own Major.    CS2 Launch: Releasing CS2 by deleting CS:GO felt like replacing a fully functioning car with a half-assembled prototype — and then setting the old car on fire so no one could go back to it. Audio broken, performance tanked, features missing… and then silence. Bravo.    You treat one of the greatest communities in gaming like we’re an inconvenience. You don’t engage, you don’t explain, and when you finally do something, it’s like you deliberately miss the point.    So again, thank you — for reminding us that no matter how good a game is, indifference from its creators will always catch up eventually.    Sincerely,  A frustrated player who keeps playing because you made something amazing — and then forgot how to care for it.

Counter-Strike 2: The Tactical Masterpiece That Ruined My Life (And I Keep Saying 'One More')    I like Counter-Strike 2. I just don’t know why. Maybe it’s the tactical gameplay that sometimes rewards strategy — usually right before my teammate rushes mid with the bomb, a dream, and no armor. Again.    The gunplay is crisp 🎯, the maps are gorgeous, and when things click, it's pure magic. But between those moments? Welcome to the Thunderdome — where your enemies are suspiciously good, your teammates are suspiciously terrible, and the AI-supported anti-cheat is just a shy spectator in the corner, taking notes and doing absolutely nothing.    Speaking of doing nothing: the report feature! It's that cute little placebo button you press after getting one-tapped through smoke by someone with a private profile and a 400-hour account. You report, smile, and imagine justice… but then remember Overwatch was removed, and nobody's actually watching. Probably not even the AI 🤖.    The community is a warm bath of toxicity ☣️, best enjoyed with earplugs and low expectations. Every match is a sociology experiment with at least one human megaphone screaming about ranks, politics, or their mother’s Wi-Fi.    And utility? A handful of players use grenades to control the map like grandmasters. The rest treat them like toys — blinding teammates, bouncing Molotovs off walls, or accidentally donating smokes to the enemy team like it’s charity 🎁.    Oh, and skins. My beautiful, pixelated financial mistake 💸. What started as one innocent case has now spiraled into a full-blown gambling addiction. I could’ve gone on vacation — instead, I own four StatTrak P250s and depression.    If you expect updates about stuff the players actually want — prepare to be amazed by yet another $3 case so Valve can milk you even more 🐄.    Still… I play. Every day. I load up, pray for a fair match, and get rewarded with emotional damage and an occasional clutch round that makes me forget everything I just said.    Final Verdict: 10/10 would suffer again.

The Good  Gunplay is still sharp.  Even with the tweaks to movement and feel, CS2 continues to deliver intense, rewarding rounds. Out-thinking and out-shooting your opponent is as satisfying as ever. The gun mechanics are still tight, and clutch moments are as exhilarating now as they were a decade ago.    The Source 2 upgrade brings visual improvements.  Volumetric smokes and updated lighting give the game a more modern look. The way utility interacts with the environment (especially how bullets and grenades now affect smoke) changes tactics in creative ways.    Matchmaking and Premier mode push the scene forward.  A global ranking system, tied to map-specific performance, is a step in the right direction. The game is clearly aimed at building a deeper competitive identity, even if it's still being refined.    Still the best when it works.  When all cylinders fire—your teammates communicate, hit reg behaves, and you’re in the zone—there’s nothing like it.    The Not-So-Good  Movement feels off.  Even after patches, something about how the player moves, jumps, and peeks feels floaty or disconnected. The CS:GO muscle memory fights against the physics in CS2. Small timings feel slightly delayed, like you’re underwater compared to the crisp precision of CS:GO.    Hit registration is inconsistent.  Sub-tick servers were promised to fix everything. Reality hasn't caught up to the marketing. Sometimes you land a perfect shot and it does nothing. Other times, you're dead before you even react. It doesn't ruin every match, but it's enough to notice—and it shouldn't be.    Missing modes and maps.  Half of the fun, casual modes from CS:GO are gone. Arms Race, Flying Scoutsman, and even classic maps like Cache and Train have vanished. If you liked anything beyond standard 5v5 competitive, your options feel severely limited.    And the Ugly: Skins  This is where it hurts. I’m someone who didn’t just play CS:GO—I lived in it. I collected skins over years. Traded, sold, bought. Not for profit, but because I loved the aesthetic, the individuality. My inventory was a digital scrapbook of my Counter-Strike experience.    When CS2 launched, the lighting overhaul and material changes completely altered how many skins look. The colors on Fades are dulled. Dopplers lost their deep, rich tones. Knives that once gleamed now look plastic or flat. The lighting engine completely changed the look of my inventory—and not for the better.    And there’s no fix. No “legacy mode.” No option to toggle the old look. Just a shrug and a patch note, and your once-rare, gorgeous skin now looks like a poorly rendered knockoff.    This isn't about money. It's about respect for time, taste, and history. I never needed skins to increase in value—but I did expect them to stay beautiful. I didn't spend hundreds of dollars to see my prized collection downgraded by a rendering engine.    Final Thoughts  CS2 is still the best tactical shooter out there. It’s the successor to a legacy title, and with time, it may surpass CS:GO in polish and popularity. The core gameplay remains addictive, challenging, and rewarding.    But if you were emotionally or financially invested in skins, just know you’re going to feel the sting. I still play, and I still love the game—but I can’t pretend the transition didn’t burn.    Recommended—but with eyes wide open.

CS2: A Problem-Filled Experience  Only you can fix this, Valve.  The game is problematic from top to bottom. AWP flick shots land behind where you're aiming. There's no optimization. Deathmatch and other modes are unplayable due to bot accounts farming weekly rewards.  The subtick system is broken. It doesn’t work as we were told — tick intervals still exist and even affect how fast we can peek in-game. Errors that never occurred on 64-tick servers happen frequently on subtick servers.  The smoke bug that was fixed in CS:GO works again in CS2. Even at the Major, bullet registration and hitbox issues occurred on LAN. So it’s not just us — the problems are clearly visible even at the professional level.  And while all this is happening, Valve releasing new skins honestly feels like mockery. None of the issues we complained about for years in CS:GO have been fixed — in fact, they’ve only much worse in CS2.  Anyway, when’s the new skin collection dropping, Valve?  Only you can fix this.

Death is a great teacher. Failure in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is, as it always has been for this series, the greatest way to learn where you should have gone, what you shouldn't have done, and how you could have done better. Counter-Strike players spend a lot of time learning -- consequently, they are always getting better.  Growth is an important factor in Global Offensive, especially if you're coming into Counter-Strike fresh or after a sabbatical. This is an extremely hardcore, skill-based first-person shooter, and it forces you to think differently than other modern shooters. If you’re a Call of Duty player, you’re going to need to change your play style to succeed here. Counter-Strike also tries developing into something new here as well, despite doing little to push itself beyond what it’s always done best. Global Offensive modifies old maps to keep veterans on their toes, and introduces official new modes that encourage different play styles for the first time in almost 15 years.  For the uninitiated, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a small-scale, team-based first-person shooter with permanent death. When a counter-terrorist kills a terrorist planting explosives in a classic Defusal match, or a CT escort swallows a sniper round in Hostage Rescue, the victim is dead for good and doesn't respawn until the next round. As such, players on both sides must exercise skill and care. The bomb objective, meanwhile, gives everyone a purpose. Of course matches end when everyone on a team is dead, but a clever and coordinated terrorist team will give the CTs the slip, plant their bomb, and protect the bomb site. Between rounds, everyone spends earned cash on better gear and guns, and the cycle continues.  Pieces of the Counter-Strike formula are dated at this point, but the superb heart and soul of Global Offensive is timeless. Teams are small, guns are lethal, and rounds are short. There's an addictive just-one-more-round quality to it, because there's a constant desire to do better than last time, to earn a satisfying kill, or to win in a new way. Call of Duty and Battlefield vets will wonder why they can't sprint to escape enemy fire or look down the iron sights to improve aim; Counter-Strike players will feel like they walked into their redecorated home. Certain map redesigns will catch hardcore fans off guard, but the changes are for the best -- the underpass choke point in de_dust, for instance, has a new escape route.  Even in the face of genre evolution, Global Offensive doesn’t care to adapt. CSGO is so dedicated to Counter-Strike's aging ideals despite market and trend changes that it brute-forces its way to success. Part of what makes it such an engaging competitive game is that killing in Global Offensive requires a wholly different skill set than other shooters. Everyone is limited to what they have and can see, with little room for character modification or on-the-fly advantages. Running and gunning is a useless play style, even if you've bought a helmet and kevlar that round, to the point that someone standing still is more likely to score the kill. Walking, crouching, or standing are your best bets to reduce the inaccurate spray of machine-gun fire.  Consequently, killing in Global Offensive feels good. There's a sickening sensation to dropping someone dead because you know they're not coming back. It's also satisfying knowing you used limited resources to play smarter than your victim. If players aren't watching corners, providing covering fire, or using smoke grenades and flashbangs, they're more likely to take a headshot from a more delicate and patient triggerman. The desire to experience that distinct feeling is a strong motivator to keep playing, even when you're getting steamrolled by an obviously better team.  If you've played Counter-Strike before, Global Offensive probably sounds a whole lot like Counter-Strike. Like Counter-Strike: Source before it, Global Offensive exists simply to modernize the look of the classic competitive shooter, while doing little to disrupt the core form and function. At the same time, it does enough to color outside the lines of tradition to justify your time and effort.  Fire is one of the most interesting new combat variables. Molotov cocktails and incendiary grenades either roast groups of guys or force them in another direction. Flames are a useful distraction or scare tactic, too. They're particularly useful during Demolition matches, which focus the fight at a single bomb site rather than giving terrorists two to pick between. The new and modified maps in this mode aren't as big as classic Counter-Strike arenas – entire sections have been cut off to direct teams toward a central location – but their thoughtful design is as intricate as ever. The Lake map is a standout -- there's a wide open yet densely populated yard around the bomb site, which is inside a sizable lakeside home with plenty of vantage points and hiding spots. To separate Demolition from Defusal, players can't buy between rounds. Instead, it takes a cue from the other new mode, Arms Race, in which each kill unlocks another weapon instantly. The better you do, the more you have to switch up the way you play, and because Demolition is so fast you'll need to be quick on your feet.  Unlike other game types, Arms Race allows for respawns. It's the most chaotic and care-free mode in Global Offensive, with players throwing caution to the wind for the sake of climbing the kill ladder as quickly as possible. It's a shame there are only two maps in Arms Race -- a problem that will more likely persist on consoles than PC.  If you have the option, playing the PC version is unquestionably the best way to experience Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. Mods, mouse and keyboard, and the usual PC-only options are better than the ports. Plus, Valve is much better about long-term PC support -- it abandoned Team Fortress 2 on consoles, and Portal 2's level editor was PC exclusive. If you prefer to play on consoles, Global Offensive is the same great game

Counter-Strike 2: A Masterpiece Marred by the Malice of Modern Gaming!  Oh, my friends, gather 'round and let me regale you with the tale of Counter-Strike 2, a game so utterly, undeniably, unequivocally magnificent that it makes the very sun seem dim by comparison! From the moment those glorious, crisp, and utterly divine new visuals graced my monitor, I knew I was in the presence of a deity. The maps, oh the maps! They breathe, they live, they shimmer with a newfound vibrancy that makes every pixel a testament to Valve's unparalleled artistry. Dust II has never looked so... dusty, yet so breathtakingly beautiful! Inferno's cobblestones gleam with a sinister allure, and Ancient's overgrown ruins whisper tales of forgotten glory with every rustling leaf. It's like stepping into a hyper-realistic painting where every headshot is a brushstroke of pure, unadulterated triumph!  The gunplay, the very soul of Counter-Strike, has been elevated to an almost spiritual plane. Every recoil pattern feels like a dance, every spray a symphony of precision. The sound design? Aural ecstasy! The satisfying thwack of a headshot, the concussive boom of a grenade, the subtle rustle of an enemy's footsteps – it's all meticulously crafted to immerse you in a ballet of bullets and tactical brilliance. And the sub-tick! Ah, the sub-tick! While I may not fully grasp its arcane sorcery, I feel it. I feel the responsiveness, the crispness, the sheer fairness of knowing that my perfect flick-shot registered with the speed of thought itself! The competitive spirit soars, the clutches are more heart-stopping, and every victory feels like conquering Everest in a single bound! CS2 isn't just a game; it's a phenomenon, a digital deity demanding worship from all who dare to enter its hallowed servers!  BUT HOLD! A dark cloud, a festering blight, a truly egregious stain mars this otherwise pristine tapestry of perfection! I speak, of course, of the infernal "gamba cases"! Oh, the audacity! To present such a divine creation, only to pollute its very essence with the predatory allure of glorified slot machines! My heart weeps, my wallet trembles, and my soul cries out in anguish as I witness fellow players succumb to the siren song of a 0.0000001% chance at a digital knife. It's a cynical, soul-crushing exploitation that cheapens the entire experience! We come for skill, for competition, for the thrill of the clutch, not to be tempted into a digital casino where the house always, always wins! Shame! Shame, I say, on this insidious practice that preys on hope and leaves only regret!  And then, the cheaters! Oh, the digital parasites! They infest the servers like a virulent plague, their aimbots and wallhacks a grotesque mockery of fair play. One moment you're executing a flawless strat, feeling like a tactical genius, the next you're insta-headshotted through three walls by an opponent whose "skill" is clearly derived from a third-party application. It's an insult to the art of competitive gaming, a slap in the face to every honest player who dedicates countless hours to honing their craft. The anti-cheat, bless its well-intentioned but seemingly impotent heart, feels like a leaky sieve against a tidal wave of malice. It sours victories, invalidates losses, and threatens to unravel the very fabric of this otherwise glorious game!  And finally, the server performance! A stutter here, a lag spike there, a sudden teleportation across the map that leaves you wondering if you've entered a dimension where ping is measured in light-years! For a game that demands split-second reactions and pixel-perfect aim, the occasional server hiccup is not merely an inconvenience; it's an act of digital sabotage! My perfectly timed peek, my meticulously planned flash, my glorious one-tap – all undone by a momentary blip in the matrix. It's a frustrating, rage-inducing flaw that snatches victory from the jaws of triumph and leaves you questioning the very stability of the digital realm!  So, there you have it. Counter-Strike 2 is a dazzling, breathtaking, almost perfect game. Its core gameplay is a masterclass, its visuals a feast for the eyes, and its potential boundless. But until Valve cleanses its soul of the insidious gamba cases, purges its servers of the cheating scourge, and fortifies its digital infrastructure against the specter of lag, it will remain a magnificent diamond with glaring, infuriating flaws. Still, I return, time and again, drawn by the irresistible pull of its brilliance, hoping one day, it will truly achieve the unblemished perfection it so tantalizingly promises!

If you’re looking for a case study in how not to manage an online multiplayer community, CS:GO is Exhibit A.  From the moment you queue into a match, you’re rolling the dice on how awful the next 30–45 minutes of your life will be. Hate speech? Common. Griefing? Constant. Team killing, doxxing threats, slurs in voice and text chat — it's all here, and it happens a lot. If you're a woman or speak with an accent? Good luck — the abuse is almost immediate.  Valve’s report system is a joke. Players who behave horrifically continue playing for weeks or months with no consequence. It’s clear that moderation is minimal at best, and nonexistent at worst. Even in “prime” matchmaking, you're just as likely to run into smurfs, cheaters, and teammates who are more interested in trolling than playing.  There’s a deeply embedded culture of hostility in the CS:GO community — not just random bad apples, but widespread, normalized toxicity. If you call someone out, you're the one who gets mass reported. If you mute people, they spam pings and throw the game. There’s no incentive to be decent, and no penalty for being awful.  Honestly, the worst part of this game isn't even the hackers or the broken matchmaking — it's the people.  Avoid this unless you're willing to play with a full team of friends every single time, or have the patience of a monk and the settings menu memorized so you can mute half the lobby before the pistol round ends.

The new Premier mode is interesting and gives a ranked grind, but the matchmaking experience can be frustrating.  CS2 has potential to surpass CS:GO, but right now it’s held back by bugs, performance issues, and a feeling that Valve rushed it out too early.  Pros:  Great graphics and updated sound design.  Volumetric smokes change the game.  Weapons feel powerful and rewarding.  Premier mode adds competitive structure.   Cons:  Movement feels clunky.  Hit registration is inconsistent. Players keep all their CS:GO items and skins. Counter-Strike is probably the most well-known FPS game or video game overall. It has a very steep learning curve and a very high skill ceiling. CS2 is a team-based shooter, where one team plays as Terrorists (T) and the other as Counter-Terrorists (CT). Communication is essential. You win the match by winning enough rounds. In CS2, the default round time is set to 2 minutes. This is the time allocated for the Terrorist team to plant the bomb or for the Counter-Terrorist team to eliminate them. Once the bomb is planted, a 40-second countdown begins  [b]Terrorists (T)[/b] win by: -Planting the bomb and having it explode. -Eliminating all Counter-Terrorists.  [b]Counter-Terrorists (CT)[/b] win by: -Defusing the planted bomb. -Preventing the bomb from being planted until the round timer ends. -Rescuing all hostages if it’s a map with hostages instead of bombsites. -Eliminating all Terrorists.  [u]Game Modes:[/u] [b]Competitive:[/b] This is the core 5v5 bomb defusal mode, focused on strategic team-based gameplay and ranking. First to 13 rounds wins.  [b]Premier:[/b] The premier competitive mode, offering a more structured and professional-level experience within the game. It involves map picking and banning before the match begins, and is considered the closest experience to pro-play. Only bomb defusal in this. First to 13 rounds unless it’s a tie 12-12, thus becoming overtime; first to 16.  [b]Wingman:[/b] A fast-paced 2v2 bomb defusal mode with a single bombsite, perfect for practicing or playing with a friend.  [b]Casual:[/b] A less intense, more relaxed version of Competitive, suitable for beginners and those looking for a casual experience.  [b]Deathmatch:[/b] A free-for-all mode where players respawn quickly and focus on practicing gunplay and improving aim.  [b]Arms Race:[/b] A fast-paced mode where players cycle through all the weapons in the game, aiming to be the first to get a kill with each weapon.   [u]Ranks:[/u] There are 18 ranks organized into six tiers: Silver, Gold Nova, Master Guardian, Legendary Eagle, Supreme Master First Class, and Global Elite. These ranks are part of the Competitive mode, and players can progress by winning matches.  Additionally, there's a Premier mode with a rating system that uses Elo points, ranging from 0 to 30000+. Your rating is recalculated after each match, and you gain or lose points based on the outcome. This rating is also color-coded, with Grey being the lowest and Dark Purple the highest.   [u]Weapons, Grenades and Skill Expression:[/u] There are many weapons in the game, all with their own learning curve and distinct “spray” pattern and recoil control. Mastering this takes a lot of time, and some never do. Aim and crosshair placement, and movement mechanics like counter-strafing and jiggle peeking are also important.  Utility tools such as grenades also exist and play a crucial role in winning rounds. You need to learn when or where to throw your frag grenades, flashbangs, molotov cocktails and smoke grenades. Smoke grenades are responsive and interact with the environment and gunfire in real-time; smoke spreads when shot or when frag grenades explode nearby.  [h2]Maps[/h2] The game takes place across 13 different maps in Competitive mode, but not all of them are active in the map pool for Premier at the same time, where they are on rotation, usually 7 maps at one time. Casual, Deathmatch and Arms Race have a few smaller and different maps. A big part of the learning curve in CS2 is learning the maps. Where and when to push, defend, throw grenades, plant the bomb, etc. All maps are distinctively different, where some are easier as T and some are easier as CT. There are tons of different tactics your team can play on each map. Map control and rotations are important regardless of which map.  [h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2] It runs on the Source 2 engine, bringing significant visual upgrades from CS:GO, such as enhanced lighting, reflections, and materials. Skins are automatically upgraded to Source 2 visuals.  The sound design is better, with a reworked sound engine that improves spatial awareness and audio clarity. Sound is a very important part of this game; hearing and locating footsteps, a T planting the bomb, a CT defusing the bomb, and more.  [h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2] The biggest issue with this game is the amount of cheaters. Not just the amount, but how long they are able to cheat without getting banned. The developers really need to step up and fix this. It’s way worse than CS:GO. This really ruins the experience and has made me quit this game several times, even though I like it.  The community and randoms are most of the time very toxic, or trolling.  [h2]The Verdict[/h2] Despite its flaws, CS2 remains one of the best competitive shooters available. For players who can handle its steep learning curve and frustrating community issues, it offers a uniquely rewarding, endlessly replayable experience that few other games can match.  [h2]Rating: 8/10[/h2]

The overwhelming number of cheaters in the competitive scene makes every match a roll of the dice, and the general lack of content and game modes from CS:GO leaves the game feeling a bit empty. It's not the polished, competitive title it could be, but for better or worse, it's the only one we have.

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) is the long-awaited continuation of the legendary shooter from Valve, replacing Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. The new Source 2 engine, updated graphics, improved physics, and new mechanics have made the game feel more modern while preserving the classic competitive shooter spirit loved by millions.  What I liked: Graphics and Visual Effects Source 2 significantly improved the game’s visuals. Maps are brighter and more detailed, models and textures look sharper. The revamped smoke grenades are especially impressive: the smoke now dynamically reacts to the environment and even to bullets and grenades, adding new tactical possibilities.  Gameplay and Physics The core gameplay remains true to the classic, which longtime CS:GO players will appreciate. At the same time, the shooting feels a bit smoother, weapon response is more precise, and movement feels more natural.  Updated Interface and Sound The interface is more modern and easier to navigate, especially for newcomers. The sound design has also been revamped: footsteps, reloads, and gunfire sound more realistic and help players better locate opponents.  Free Upgrade from CS:GO CS:GO players automatically receive access to CS2, making the transition seamless and free.  What I didn’t like: Launch Issues Like many major releases, CS2 had technical issues during its initial weeks: bugs, inconsistent performance, and criticism from the esports community due to missing features and maps.  Lack of Content at Launch Some classic maps and game modes were missing at launch, which disappointed part of the community. Valve is gradually restoring content and has promised ongoing updates.  Optimization CS2 can run worse than CS:GO on lower-end or even mid-range PCs, which frustrated some users. However, future patches are expected to improve this.

🚗💥 PUBG – Battle Royale? Nah, More Like Betrayal Royale 🔫🤣  Everyone else loads up PUBG with dreams of chicken dinners, tactical gunfights, and glorious long-range headshots. Not me. No, my fun came from being the true final boss of every squad I joined — the guy my teammates should have been watching out for instead of the enemy.  Sure, PUBG is technically a serious, tactical shooter. Massive maps, realistic gunplay, intense firefights. But all of that fades into background noise the moment you’re behind the wheel of a rusty Dacia and your “allies” are lined up on the road ahead. There’s no thrill quite like hearing “Wait—WAIT—STOP—” in voice chat right before you floor it and send your entire squad ragdolling into the afterlife.  Sometimes I’d switch it up — a grenade “accidentally” tossed into a building they were looting, a well-placed shotgun blast in the back “to check if friendly fire was on,” or just slowly driving away with the only vehicle while they bled out. Every match became less about surviving the circle and more about seeing just how far I could push my chaos before someone rage quit.  Was it productive? Absolutely not. Did it ruin games? Completely. Was it some of the most fun I’ve ever had in an online shooter? You bet your last medkit it was.  PUBG gave me freedom — the freedom to betray, to troll, to weaponize every vehicle on the map, and to make sure no one in my squad ever trusted random teammates again.  10/10 – Didn’t win a single chicken dinner, but feasted daily on the salty tears of betrayed comrades. 🚗💀🎤

Micro transactions suck major ass, any good skin is locked behind paywalls, which make them worth pennies once you spend a few bucks. After opening hundreds of free crates and event items I haven't managed to get a single progressive skin which they have a whole section of the menu dedicated to.  All in all its a free game now can't complain much about that.

Hours played: Too many.  Friends made: Lifelong.  Sanity left: Minimal. Recommended: No  I’ve been playing PUBG since season one, day one. Back when frying pans were sacred, Erangle felt like a cursed second home, and the most dangerous thing on the map was your ears getting destroyed by global voice chat in the loading lobby. I've made lifelong friends, laughed more times than i can count, and screamed in joy after clutching that last 1v1 chicken dinner.  But that game? That magical, janky, adrenaline-fueled chaos? It’s dead now. Buried beneath a swamp of hackers, aimbots, and broken dreams.  The devs? Well, they don’t seem to care. Instead of fixing the infestation of cheaters that now make up half the player base, they spend their time churning out overpriced battle passes and skins that look like they were rejected from Fortnite’s toddler collection. I didn’t support and play this game for years just to get head shot by a guy wearing a unicorn onesie from 600m away with a pistol. BUT WAIT! I got a ban report.... 24 hr ban for blatant cheating...  Remember when we used to drop into Pochinki and pray we found a level 3 helmet? Now I drop in and pray I get five minutes of gameplay before some hacker turns me into loot.  PUBG gave me some of the best gaming memories of my life. And now it’s giving me the worst.  Rest in peace, old friend. You deserved better.
